topics.title: Introduction to Financing Working Capital
explain: After estimating required working capital, the finance manager must arrange appropriate funding.
Permanent working capital is needed continuously and should be financed via long-term sources like debt and equity.
Temporary working capital fluctuates with sales and should be financed through short-term sources.
Sources of short-term finance are broadly grouped into Spontaneous sources and Negotiated sources.
Key decision parameters include cost, impact on credit rating, feasibility, reliability, restrictions, and hedging/matching approach.

flow.title: Working Capital Financing Decision Process
steps: Bifurcate capital into permanent and temporary
Match permanent needs with long-term funds
Match temporary needs with short-term funds
Evaluate sources on cost and credit rating
Select optimal mix of spontaneous and negotiated funds

topics.example: A retail store uses long-term equity to buy permanent store fixtures and short-term bank credit to purchase extra holiday season inventory.
remember: Matching approach -> Match asset maturity with funding maturity
mistakes: Financing permanent working capital with short-term loans, which creates liquidity risks.

quiz.q: How should permanent working capital ideally be financed?
o: Long-term sources like debt and equity
quiz.why: Permanent working capital is continuously required irrespective of sales fluctuations, so it requires long-term financing.

quiz.q: Which parameter advocates matching the maturity of financing with the maturity of assets?
quiz.why: The hedging or matching approach aligns asset maturities with the maturity of their funding sources.

topics.title: Spontaneous Sources of Finance
explain: Spontaneous sources naturally arise in the routine course of business operations without formal negotiations.
Trade Credit is extended by sellers/service providers and covers about one-third of short-term financing needs.
Open account trade credit allows purchases without extensive documentation.
Bills Payable involves a written promise to pay the seller on demand or at a specified future date.
Accrued Expenses (like unpaid wages, salaries, and taxes) act as an automatic, interest-free source of short-term finance.

flow.title: Mechanism of Spontaneous Financing
steps: Business conducts routine operational activities
Goods/services received from suppliers or employees
Payment deferred to agreed future date or end of period
Funds retained in business interest-free during credit period
Dues cleared at the end of credit term

topics.example: A factory receives raw materials on 30-day credit from a supplier, allowing it to generate cash from sales before paying the bill.
remember: Trade Credit covers ~1/3rd of total short-term requirements
Accrued Expenses represent interest-free built-in finance
mistakes: Thinking spontaneous sources require formal loan negotiations with commercial banks.

quiz.q: What proportion of short-term funding requirements is typically contributed by trade credit?
quiz.why: Trade credit is a major short-term source contributing about one-third of total short-term requirements.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an interest-free, built-in spontaneous source of finance?
quiz.why: Accrued expenses like unpaid wages or taxes are automatic, interest-free sources of finance.

topics.title: Commercial Papers and Inter-Corporate Deposits
explain: Inter-Corporate Loans and Deposits occur when companies with surplus funds invest short-term with other entities at higher interest rates than bank deposits.
Commercial Paper (CP) is an unsecured promissory note issued by highly rated corporates to raise short-term funds.
Maturity period for Commercial Paper ranges from a minimum of 7 days to less than 1 year.
Commercial Paper is issued in minimum denominations of ₹5 lakhs or multiples thereof.
CP offers lower interest costs than bank loans, but is restricted only to corporate entities with high credit ratings.

flow.title: Issuance of Commercial Paper
steps: Highly rated corporate assesses short-term liquidity need
Issues unsecured promissory notes in multiples of ₹5 lakhs
Investors purchase CP in money market
Funds utilized for operational needs (7 days to <1 year)
Redeemed at maturity or rolled over with new issue

topics.example: A AAA-rated company issues ₹50 lakhs worth of Commercial Paper for 90 days at a 6.5% interest rate to meet working capital needs.
remember: CP Minimum Denomination = ₹5 lakhs or multiples thereof
CP Maturity Range = 7 days to less than 1 year
Issuer Requirement = Highly credit-rated firms only
mistakes: Assuming new or poorly rated firms can easily issue Commercial Paper to solve liquidity problems.

quiz.q: What is the minimum maturity period for Commercial Paper?
quiz.why: Commercial Paper maturity ranges from a minimum of 7 days to less than 1 year.

quiz.q: In what denomination can Commercial Papers be issued?
quiz.why: CP can be issued in denominations of ₹5 lakhs or multiples thereof.

topics.title: Other Short-Term Sources, Bills Schemes & Factoring
explain: Funds generated from operations (profit and depreciation) increase working capital.
Public Deposits are short-to-medium term deposits raised from the general public by well-established companies.
Bills Discounting involves selling an accepted bill of exchange to a bank before maturity to get immediate cash.
Reserve Bank of India introduced the Bill Rediscounting Scheme w.e.f. 1st November 1970 for licensed scheduled banks.
Factoring is an arrangement where a firm sells its receivables at a discount to a factor who manages debt collection.
Factoring (Invoice factoring) has no specific Act, whereas Bills Discounting (Invoice discounting) falls under the Negotiable Instruments Act.

flow.title: Factoring vs Bills Discounting Mechanism
steps: Firm sells goods on credit to buyer
In Factoring: Sales ledger & debts transferred to factor
In Bills Discounting: Bill drawn, accepted & discounted with bank
Intermediary provides immediate funds against receivables
Debts collected by factor/bank on due date

topics.example: A firm sells receivables of ₹10 lakhs to a factoring company which advances 80% upfront and handles collection from debtors.
remember: Bill Rediscounting Scheme introduced by RBI on 1st November 1970
Factoring = Invoice Factoring (Parties: Client, Factor, Debtor)
Bills Discounting = Invoice Discounting (Governed by Negotiable Instruments Act)
mistakes: Confusing parties in factoring (Client, Factor, Debtor) with parties in bills discounting (Drawer, Drawee, Payee).

quiz.q: When was the Bill Rediscounting Scheme introduced by the Reserve Bank of India?
quiz.why: The Bill Rediscounting Scheme was introduced by RBI w.e.f. 1st November 1970.

quiz.q: Which governing legal framework applies to Bills Discounting but NOT to Factoring?
quiz.why: Bills Discounting is governed by the Negotiable Instruments Act, while Factoring has no specific dedicated Act.

topics.title: Bank Finance and Forms of Bank Credit
explain: Commercial banks are major suppliers of working capital credit in India; Tandon and Chore Committees laid early guidelines.
In April 1997, RBI withdrew mandatory Maximum Permissible Bank Finance (MPBF) norms, giving banks freedom to frame board-approved lending policies.
Cash Credit: Continuous credit facility up to a sanctioned limit.
Bank Overdraft: Short-term borrowing facility for urgent needs with bank's right to call back at short notice.
Bills Acceptance: Company draws bill on bank, bank accepts promising payment on a future date.
Line of Credit & Letter of Credit: Commitment to lend on demand up to a maximum limit, or guarantee of payment against stipulated documents.
Bank Guarantee: Bank undertakes responsibility on behalf of client in favour of third-party beneficiaries.

flow.title: Bank Credit Assessment and Financing Flow
steps: Borrower applies to bank for working capital credit
Bank assesses working capital needs per board-approved policy
Bank sanctions credit limit (Cash Credit / Overdraft / LC)
Borrower draws funds up to sanctioned limit
Bank monitors credit compliance and exposure norms

topics.example: A manufacturing firm uses a Cash Credit account to draw funds up to ₹50 lakhs for raw material purchases, paying interest only on the utilized amount.
remember: RBI withdrew MPBF concept in April 1997
Cash Credit = Continuous borrowing facility up to sanctioned limit
Bank Overdraft = Short-term emergency facility callable at short notice
mistakes: Believing that MPBF calculation guidelines issued by RBI remain compulsory for bank lending today.

quiz.q: When did RBI withdraw the mandatory prescription of Maximum Permissible Bank Finance (MPBF)?
quiz.why: RBI withdrew mandatory MPBF prescriptions in April 1997, giving banks autonomy.

quiz.q: Which facility allows a borrower continuous credit up to a sanctioned ceiling from a bank?
quiz.why: Cash credit is a continuous credit facility provided by bankers up to a sanctioned limit.
